utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there is no procedural matter to be raised, we'll move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DST-044. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Groome will continue his cross-examination. Mr. Groome, the Chamber considered yesterday the issue raised by Mr. Jordash, discussed during the last five minutes. You may put to the witness what you find in the statement you refer to. However, it should be perfectly clear that there could be no suggestion going beyond what is actually found in that statement. So nothing about conversations if it's not there. So it should be perfectly clear. And, Mr. Jordash, if you find anything in that statement you would like do put to the witness where you consider that he might shed some additional light on matters, then you are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to be sure that I understand the Chamber's Ruling, that not to characterise anything found in that statement as an indication that a conversation took place, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's whether it's in relation to time of conversation, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can put to the witness what is found in that statement but without any suggestion as to where it comes from or what was the situation in which he gained any information. So strictly limited to what you find in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber wonders whether we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the -- a unit referred to as Plavci? Or Plavsi? I'm not sure about my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you just to say the name of the unit that I -- that you think you heard me say, just to confirm that I have pronounced it correctly. What's the name of the unit that I've just asked you about? Or perhaps a better way for me to do it is just to simply spell it: P-l-a-v-c-i.

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. S, not C, Plavci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Have you heard of that unit?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, never. I never heard of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that D31 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is an information report issued by Major-General Mile Babic, commander of the 1st District security organ on the 19th of October, 1991. Now, in it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, now I've omitted the reference that I need. Oh, I'm sorry. In the third paragraph. If we can look down at the third paragraph in both. I think on the English we need to go to the second page. I apologise to the Chamber. I'm thinking about a different document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my last question to you, or last series of questions to you, I want to return to the men at Pajzos. Can you describe for us their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore what, at the time, were regular, standard-issue, camouflage military uniforms. And what distinguished them from the others were the red berets which they wore on their heads. And all wore them, without exception.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they refer to themselves, their unit, by the name "Red Berets"?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The red berets on their heads were a signal, a sort of a signal, to the environment. If they had worn blue berets, we would probably have called them Blue Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that P2158 be brought to our screens, and could I ask that we go immediately to page 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you see this exhibit on the screen before you, it is a composite exhibit that includes a number of photographs of men in uniform. Could I ask you to look at it and, once you have, to tell us whether the uniforms Bozovic and his men were wearing in Pajzos are similar to those we see on page 3 of P2158.

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. These uniforms that I see now are of a more recent type. And the only similarities are that they are both camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the beret that the men are wearing in these photographs, in particular the insignia that we see on them; do you recognise that from the men in Pajzos?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The berets were red. As for the insignia, I'm almost certain that they had no such insignia on their berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, DST-044.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no more questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to address you, if I may, on Rule 90(H) in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break anyhow soon, I would say. So, therefore, perhaps we could already ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. And we'd like to see you back after the break, Witness DST-044, which might take another -- a little bit over half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at D68. It's about to come up on our screen. Can you please look at this exhibit. It's a short one. Please read it. There's a reference here to patrol activity in Sarengrad at the Bapska cross-roads. Can you tell us where this junction is in relation to Pajzos, geographically speaking?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the report when I came here. This is the portion of the road leading into Pajzos itself, but they didn't control that area at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," you mean the group at Pajzos; right?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the group and also the person who signed the document, if, indeed, he was there, was he a member of that group. But he couldn't have been someone from the police units, the units under the police station. I would have known of him. But they certainly weren't patrolling that particular area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The header reads that this is a report produced by the Republic of Serbian Krajina Ministry of the Interior Ilok Special-Purpose Unit. You never saw any ID or any proof offered by those men. Do you allow for the possibility that this group was perhaps a part of some special-purpose unit of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particular in view of the date that I see there. At the time, the Republic of Krajina operated more and more, in terms of its MUP being fully functional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have any questions. Mr. Groome, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just -- let me -- I'm just still trying to digest, Your Honour, the last couple of questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could just ask a question, a few questions, regarding the last couple of questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the last answer that you gave to Mr. Petrovic, you said: "... in particular in view of the date that I see there." Does that mean that your answer, the evidence that you've given, relates to the document that's now on our screen, this exhibit? D68?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the report that I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So when Mr. Petrovic asked you: "Do you allow for the possibility that this group was perhaps a part of some special ... unit of the ..." and then we don't have the rest of the question, when you said "yes," you were referring to the people that are described in D68?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the report when I came here, and I was shown the report. Then I compared the substance and signature, a person I don't know, and in the heading, the date and everything, by this time the MUP of the Krajina had already been set up and fully operating, and they may have started some regular activities as a regular unit at Pajzos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe I've cleared that up, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I have one question or a series of questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have extensively answered questions about your encounter with Mr. Stanisic, which took place at a checking point nearby Ilok on the route from Sid to Backa Palanka. You remember?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand your testimony well that it was purely coincidental that you, there, met Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was on a controlled tour of the check-point. The policeman pulled over a small white vehicle, a small jeep, and the policeman said, Come over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I saw in your statement that your answers are slightly different from your testimony given today, mainly in the area of who told who what. In your statement, it's Jovica Stanisic who told you about the problems in Mohovo and Bapska and about the pressure Croats and Slovaks were exposed to. Now, today, it -- I understood your testimony mainly to be that you told him about these kind of problems. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly. But he asked me, when we met, if there were any problems involving the Slovaks. The emphasise was always on the Slovaks. Then I told him, as I said today, that, yes, there were problems, that I had problems bordering on incidents in the villages of Bapska and Mohovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you apparently then exchanged views on these matters. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he suggested the solutions to you, either directly or indirectly. Is that also well understood?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He indirectly proposed solutions. It was a mere suggestion. No more than that. But I was an experienced professional, and I knew how to take a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, people might wonder and consider it very coincidental that you, as a pure coincidence, happened to see Mr. Stanisic, that you briefly discuss a matter on which you apparently had not taken action before, and then take action upon suggestions made, although indirectly, to you on how to resolve this matter. Why had you not acted before?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. Previous to this indirect suggestion, I hadn't taken any steps. Prior to our meeting, that is. The reason being, I believed the incidents in those two villages to be marginal as compared to the overall security situation. They hadn't escalated that far. This, however, was a signal for me, a reliable signal, that it was time to prevent any possible escalation of the clashes there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you gave all the information to Mr. Stanisic, or was he aware of these problems?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he indirectly suggested this to me, so logic dictates that he probably had an idea about it. He had someone from the service there that I mentioned, Mr. Sarac, who was monitoring the situation throughout. There was nothing alarming about what was going on, but it strikes me as quite certain that Mr. Stanisic was already in possession of that information which I then confirmed for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you, purely coincidental, meet Mr. Stanisic. You give him -- when he asked you to tell about the situation, and then you -- he apparently is already aware of all the problems, then you said: "... which I then confirmed for him." At the same time, you tell us that you were the one who informed Mr. Stanisic about the problems. At least that's what we hear in your testimony and which is not in your statement. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: DST-044 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not in the statement because I wasn't asked specifically, about the meeting, the sort of specific question that I received today. I answered the question as it was asked. I don't think it's contradictory. And I think I've just had a chance to explain it fully.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was -- had informally inquired with the Prosecution how much time you would need, Mr. Groome, for cross-examination, and I think you performed quicker than announced. And on the basis of the time we would expect to need for re-examination and questions by the Chamber and potentially further cross-examination, we considered that the next witness should not wait. If we would have known how matters had developed, we might have taken a different decision as far as the -- whether the witness should remain stand-by or not, because we're losing more or less half an hour which we hardly can afford. I leave it to that for the time being, but I encourage the parties that even if this information is given informally, that it should be reliable to the extent possible. We adjourn for the day. And we'll resume tomorrow morning, Wednesday, the 24th of August, and 9.00 in this same Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of August, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.42 p.m.,
